newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Would-be Hong Kong leaders hard to tell apart.
newsitem.headline: Would-be Hong Kong leaders hard to tell apart.

text.p: There is little to distinguish between the four front-runners vying to step into Governor Chris Patten's shoes when the British haul down their flag and hand over Hong Kong to China next year.
All are men. When it comes to family background the scale runs from extremely wealthy to fabulously rich.
Although three were born in Shanghai and one in Hong Kong, all have received at least part of their education overseas and are equally at home in English and Chinese.
Neither is there much that distinguishes between them when it comes to politics.
None are tub thumpers advocating startling change in the years following the handover at midnight on June 30 next year.
All four stress caution, the need for stability during the delicate early years as Hong Kong, a British colony for over a century and a half, adjusts to once again being a part of China.

All four candidates have dodged questions on democracy and civil liberties in the territory after the handover but have said they would work with the Provisional Legislature which Beijing wants to set up to replace Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council.
In age they range from 50 to 74. Two ran family business empires. Two hail from the top tier of the Hong Kong judiciary.
Hong Kong, which returned its first all-elected legislature only last year, faces a month-long election-style blitz, even though the first post-colonial leader will be chosen and not elected.
Of 31 candidates, opinion polls show outgoing Chief Justice Sir Ti Liang Yang, 67, ahead by a nose over billionaire shipping tycoon Tung Chee-wah, 59 who leads businessman Peter Woo, 50.
In fourth place is former Appeal Court Judge Simon Li, at 74, the oldest candidate and the last to declare.
If the people of Hong Kong were to choose, they would plump for none of them.
Instead, as regular opinion polls have showed, the most popular choice was Patten's female deputy, the head of Hong Kong's 180,000-strong civil service, Anson Chan.
Chan, however, ruled herself out before the nomination period ended at 5 pm (0900 GMT) on Monday.

"After careful consideration of all the relevant factors governing the selection process and having consulted my senior colleagues within the civil service, I have decided not to put my name forward as a candidate for the chief executive post," she announced on Saturday.
She did however express her desire to continue to serve Hong Kong and many civil servants say they hope she will stay on in her post as the territory's top mandarin.
Hong Kong's new leader will be chosen by a 400-member electoral college currently being assembled by China's handpicked Preparatory Committee.

Hong Kong people know the man named in December will be the choice of China's leaders but that has not prevented the leading candidates from hitting the hustings as if their future lay directly in the hands of the voters.
They know they must demonstrate to Beijing's ageing leaders that they enjoy at least a semblance of public support.
They have already begun jostling for the front pages by laying out policy platforms, struggling to talk in soundbites and employing spin-doctors and photo-opportunities to attract the media.
Hong Kong's pro-democracy politicians, who have boycotted the event on the grounds the future leader should be elected and not selected, have been quick to point out the irony.
"The media in general are insulting the intelligence of Hong Kong people because by and large they present this thing as a race," said independent legislator Emily Lau.
"They say there is a very heated contest going on but they know as much as all of us know there is no race as such because only Beijing and Beijing alone decides," she added.
